documented.label: Documented
documented.text: An official record, court ruling, statute or direct count shows this happened or exists. The label says nothing about the size of an effect unless the record does.

well-supported.label: Well supported
well-supported.text: Strong evidence backs the direction of the effect: a well-designed study such as a randomized experiment, several consistent studies, or an official estimate made with a published method. No credible study finds the opposite.

plausible.label: Plausible
plausible.text: The mechanism is coherent and some evidence points this way. The studies are few, weak in design or limited to some places.

contested.label: Contested
contested.text: Credible studies disagree. The record shows both sides.

hypothesis.label: Hypothesis
hypothesis.text: A proposed explanation that has not been tested. It is never the only support for a claim.

not yet tested.label: Not yet tested
not yet tested.text: No evaluation of this response's effects exists yet.

mixed.label: Mixed
mixed.text: The evidence points in different directions for different parts of the claim.

quotes.outside_driver_glossary: A force that affects the model but whose own causes lie outside its boundary, such as technology, population patterns, trade, foreign interference and major shocks. Drawn as a rounded pill outside the clusters.
quotes.confidence_label_glossary: The short label on a claim or response saying what kind of evidence supports it: documented, well-supported, plausible, contested, hypothesis or not yet tested. The same scale grades connections on the map.
quotes.connection_glossary: A claimed relationship between two variables. Its record explains the mechanism, gives the evidence grade and states the delay. Connection IDs begin with L, LE, LT, LX or T.
quotes.issue_record_glossary: One of 193 records beneath the map, with IDs such as I017 or X01. Each describes a documented problem, case or policy, names its mechanism, gives an evidence grade, status and sources, and links to a variable or connection where it can.
quotes.well_supported_glossary: The confidence label for a relationship on which several credible studies, designed to rule out other explanations, agree about direction. Each study's setting and limits still apply.
quotes.documented_glossary: The confidence label for a fact or event on the public record: a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic. It establishes the event; it says nothing about the size of an effect unless the record does.
quotes.hypothesis_glossary: The confidence label for a proposed relationship that needs stronger evidence. Diagrams draw it as a dotted line, and it never serves as the only support for a claim.
quotes.authority_glossary: A connection showing that one body holds legal power over something: it appoints, appropriates, preempts, enforces or sets a rate. It says who decides, without saying which way the decision goes, so it has no sign and never closes a loop.
quotes.delay_glossary: The time between a change and its effect. Codes: S, under 2 years; M, 2 to 10 years; L, over 10 years.
quotes.loop_closure_glossary: A complete path of connections that returns to the starting variable. If any closing step is only a hypothesis, the whole loop stays uncertain.
quotes.positive_sign_glossary: The connected variables tend to move in the same direction, with the model's other conditions held steady. A positive sign does not mean a benefit.
quotes.repair_log_glossary: A dated list of 64 rule changes that altered who officials answer to, coded toward voters, away from voters, voters kept existing rules, mixed or pending.
quotes.methods_documented: Documented means the event or fact is on the public record, such as a statute, a court ruling or an official statistic;
quotes.methods_well_supported: Well supported means strong evidence backs the direction: a well-designed study such as a randomized experiment, several consistent studies, or an official estimate made with a published method, with no credible study finding the opposite.
quotes.methods_plausible: Plausible means the mechanism is coherent and some evidence points that way, though the studies are weak or few.
quotes.methods_mixed: Mixed means the evidence points in different directions for different parts of a claim.
quotes.methods_contested: Contested means credible studies disagree, and both sides appear with the claim.
quotes.methods_hypothesis: Hypothesis marks a proposed mechanism the model needs and cannot yet support;
quotes.methods_identifiers: Identifiers are exact: R-05 is a reform profile and R5 is a loop, and a code such as B2 can name a variable (local reporting) or a loop (automatic benefits), so the text always says which.
quotes.methods_authority: They record who holds legal power over something, such as Congress appropriating research money, without saying which way the decision will go, so they carry no sign and never close a loop.
quotes.methods_sign: a plus sign can mark a harmful effect.
quotes.methods_no_score: The Atlas does not predict elections or the odds that a reform passes, add reform effects into a single score, rank candidates or parties, or estimate how strong a whole loop is.
quotes.outcomes_why_not_one_number: The four outcome families use different units. A reform can improve one while imposing a cost on another, and the evidence behind each estimate differs in quality. Keeping the families separate lets readers see those tradeoffs; adding them into one score would hide them.
quotes.effect_codes_note: Reform profiles use these codes to show the expected direction and rough size of an effect on each outcome family. The codes are conditional on the reform working as described, and codes for different families are never added together.
quotes.repair_coding_last: A row's direction describes the rule's effect on who officials answer to and carries no judgment of the people or parties involved.
quotes.delivery_grade_note: The evidence grade on each entry rates the measured result;

L02.name: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors
L02.qualification: A 2016 field experiment (Kalla and Broockman) found congressional offices granted meetings more often to people identified as donors; affluent and middle-income Americans want the same policy about 90% of the time, so any tilt shows on the issues where they differ.

L09.qualification: Contested. R1.title: Wealth and political influence reinforce each other
R1.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R1.evidence_summary: The first and last steps are well supported: L01: Concentrated wealth funds more political spending rests on donor records, and L03: Policy advantages add to wealth at the top on CBO's accounting of who receives tax benefits. The middle step, L02: Political spending can tilt policy toward donors, is plausible and the weakest. A 2016 field experiment found that donors get meetings, and since affluent and middle-income Americans want the same policy about 90% of the time, any tilt shows only where they disagree.
R1.qualification: The loop runs on issues where wealthy donors' preferences differ from those of middle-income voters; on most issues the two groups agree, so its reach depends on the issue.

R8.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R8.evidence: well-supported for both links; the loop no longer depends on A1
R8.evidence_summary: Both steps are well supported. L38: Scarcity raises existing home values rests on house-price studies and the owner-renter wealth gap in the Survey of Consumer Finances (1989 to 2022). L39: Owners' equity drives opposition to new housing rests on homevoter research (Fischel 2001) and records of Massachusetts planning meetings (Einstein, Glick and Palmer 2019); it is the weaker step because equity is one motive among several for opposing construction.

B4.title: Electoral consequences can improve public performance
B4.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
B4.evidence: well-supported where seats are competitive; C5 to D5 well-supported
B4.evidence_summary: All three steps are well supported: retrospective voting in L23: Poor service raises incumbents' risk of losing, defeats where seats are competitive in L24: Electoral pressure leads to actual defeats, and better performance after replacement or its threat in L54: Removing incumbents improves performance of those remaining. For U.S. services the weakest is L54, since its main study covers Brazilian mayors.
B4.qualification: The loop works only where seats are competitive. The threat of defeat and an actual defeat are separate steps, and testing the loop needs evidence on both over several election cycles.

link_detail.qualification: Retrospective voting is well documented (Healy and Malhotra 2013), and voters also punish officials for events outside their control, such as natural disasters, so the pressure does not track performance alone.

link_detail.name: Electoral pressure leads to actual defeats
link_detail.qualification: Pressure can change an official's behavior before any defeat occurs, so testing the whole chain needs evidence on both the threat and the defeats over several election cycles.

link_detail.name: Removing incumbents improves performance of those remaining
link_detail.qualification: The main study (Ferraz and Finan 2011) found that Brazilian mayors who could run again misused less federal money than mayors facing term limits; U.S. service quality was not studied.

R11.title: Party loyalty weakens consequences for breaking norms
R11.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R11.evidence: well-supported for B4 to C3; plausible for the rest
R11.evidence_summary: Survey experiments (Graham and Svolik 2020) give strong support to L50: Partisan loyalty shields incumbents from voter punishment, and studies of presidential power back L51: Electoral pressure restrains unilateral presidential action (Howell 2003; Christenson and Kriner 2020). The weakest step is L52: Unilateral action deepens partisan hostility, graded plausible, which rests on social identity research (Mason 2018) without a direct test.

R7.title: Service performance and earned trust can reinforce each other
R7.closure: closed: every step is a numbered connection
R7.evidence: hypothesis for the named direction; plausible for the compliance channel; the delivery leg is documented case by case in the Delivery Log, though no study measures the loop closing
R7.evidence_summary: Both steps are graded plausible. In L20: Better public services build earned trust, survey trust also moves with which party holds office (Hetherington 2005). B2.title: Automatic benefits cushion economic shocks
B2.evidence_summary: The model grades the mechanism well supported. Neither step is a numbered connection with its own citation, so the evidence cannot be inspected step by step, and that missing chain is the weakest point.
B2.qualification: Only benefits with triggers in law respond automatically. The 2021 expanded child tax credit was a one-year decision that expired on a set date, so it shows what a permanent design could do without being an instance of one.

B3.title: New competitors can limit market power
B3.evidence_summary: The model grades the mechanism well supported where entry is possible. Its three variables sit outside the model's numbered variables and none of its steps is a numbered connection, so the weakest point is the missing chain.
B3.qualification: Entry needs access, financing and scale, and vertical integration or serial acquisitions can block it, so high profits in a concentrated market do not guarantee that a rival appears.

R9.title: Taking part in a successful repair may support the next one
R9.evidence_summary: The complete loop is a design hypothesis. Studies of citizen panels and participatory budgeting measure effects on participants, and the weakest step is the return from trust to wider participation, which has not been measured across the population.
R9.qualification: Effects are measured on the people who took part; evidence of lasting change in the wider public's trust or participation is limited.

scale.high: The route is open, and the reform has been adopted somewhere through it since 2020.
scale.medium: The route is open in some places, and a credible campaign could carry the reform through it by 2030.
scale.low: The route exists, but it needs a coalition that does not exist now.

rows.rule: The Voting Rights Act banned discriminatory voting tests and required places with a history of discrimination to get federal approval (preclearance) before changing voting rules.

New York City Local Law 8 of 1988 created the Campaign Finance Board and a public matching-funds program for small contributions, first paid at 1 to 1 in 1989 and raised to 4 to 1 in 1998, 6 to 1 in 2007 and 8 to 1 from 2019. A charter referendum on November 8, 1988 then made the Board an independent agency under the City Charter, so a later Council could not simply repeal it.
Citizens United v. FEC held that limits on independent political spending by corporations and unions violate the First Amendment.
Shelby County v. Holder struck down the Section 4(b) coverage formula, ending Section 5 preclearance in practice.
McCutcheon v. FEC struck down aggregate limits on how much one donor may give to all federal candidates and parties combined.

HB 2177 made Oregon the first state to register eligible voters automatically from driver license records. By the National Conference of State Legislatures' count of August 19, 2026, 24 states and the District of Columbia have enacted or put in place automatic voter registration.

Question 5 adopted ranked-choice voting, in which voters rank candidates and ballots transfer when a first choice is eliminated, for state and federal primaries and for general elections for U.S. Senate, U.S. House, governor and the legislature.
LD 1646 delayed ranked-choice voting until December 2021 and repealed it automatically unless voters amended the state constitution.

Question 1, a people's veto (a referendum that lets voters repeal a law the legislature passed), overturned the legislature's 2017 delay-and-repeal law and restored ranked-choice voting for primaries and federal general elections.
Proposal 2 created a 13-member independent citizens redistricting commission to draw congressional and legislative maps.
Proposition 4 created an independent redistricting commission and banned partisan gerrymandering in the drawing of congressional and legislative districts.
Charter Question 1 raised the public match to 8-to-1 on small contributions and lowered contribution limits for city offices.

Utah S.B. 200 turned the redistricting commission created by Proposition 4 into a seven-member advisory body appointed largely by legislative leaders, and let the Legislature vote on or adopt a commission map without being required to. It also dropped Proposition 4's partisan-fairness standard and its route to court review.

Ballot Measure 2 replaced party primaries with a top-four open primary (all candidates on one ballot, with the top four advancing), adopted ranked-choice voting for general elections and required disclosure of the true source of large political contributions.
The American Rescue Plan raised the child tax credit to $3,600 for young children and $3,000 for older children, made it fully refundable, and paid half in monthly installments for 2021 only.
The expanded child tax credit expired, returning the credit to $2,000 per child with refunds capped at $1,500 per child for 2022.
Question 3, a constitutional amendment for top-five open primaries and ranked-choice general elections, passed its first of two required votes.
The Securing Inspector General Independence Act required the President to give Congress 30 days' notice and a substantive, case-specific reason before removing an inspector general.
The Electoral Count Reform Act made the Vice President's role ministerial and raised the threshold to object to electoral votes to one-fifth of each chamber.

The Utah Supreme Court held unanimously that the legislature may not repeal or impair a voter-approved government-reform initiative unless narrowly tailored to a compelling interest, reviving the challenge to SB 200.
Ballot Measure 2 to repeal the top-four primary and ranked-choice voting failed, keeping the 2020 system in place.
CI-126, which would have created a top-four open primary for state and federal offices, was defeated.
CI-127, which would have required a majority vote to win statewide and legislative elections, was defeated.
Proposition 1, a top-four primary with ranked-choice general elections, was defeated.
Proposition 131, a top-four primary with ranked-choice general elections, was defeated.

Nevada Question 3 would have replaced closed party primaries with one open primary for all candidates, the top five advancing, and required ranked-choice voting in general elections for federal and statewide offices. Nevada requires two votes for a citizen-initiated constitutional amendment; this was the second, after the first passed in 2022 with 52.94%.
Measure 117, ranked-choice voting for federal and statewide offices beginning 2028, was defeated.
Proposition 140, a single open primary for all candidates with possible ranked-choice general elections, was defeated.
Initiative 83 adopted ranked-choice voting beginning in 2026 and opened party primaries to voters not registered with a party, subject to funding by the D.C. Council.
Amendment 7 wrote a ban on ranked-choice voting into the state constitution and required plurality primary winners to be the sole nominee.
The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau finalized a rule treating overdraft fees at large banks as credit under the Truth in Lending Act unless capped at $5 or priced at cost.
The White House removed at least 17 inspectors general by email, effective immediately, without the 30 days' notice or case-specific reason the statute requires.

Executive Order 14248 directed the Election Assistance Commission to require documentary proof of citizenship on the federal voter registration form and to penalize states that count mail ballots received after Election Day.
S.J.Res.18 nullified the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's overdraft rule under the Congressional Review Act and barred a substantially similar rule.

P.L. 119-21 set the child tax credit at up to $2,200 per child. At most $1,700 of it is refundable (paid to families whose credit exceeds the income tax they owe), and the refundable part requires at least $2,500 in earnings, so the full refundability of 2021 was not restored.
The D.C. Council voted 8-4 to fund ranked-choice voting implementation for the June 2026 primary, while withholding funds for semi-open primaries until June 2026.
Proposition 1 renewed the Democracy Voucher property tax levy for ten years starting 2026 to keep funding four $25 vouchers per resident per election.
HB 4 enacted a mid-decade congressional map designed to move five seats held by Democrats to Republicans.

In Storch v. Hegseth Judge Ana Reyes said the January 2025 removals of inspectors general almost undoubtedly violated the Inspector General Act, but denied reinstatement because the President could remove them again after giving proper notice. The court then paused the case until the Supreme Court decided Trump v. Slaughter (June 29, 2026).
HB 1 (2025 Second Extraordinary Session) enacted a mid-decade congressional map splitting Kansas City among three districts to change control of the 5th District.
Proposition 50 temporarily transferred congressional redistricting from the independent Citizens Redistricting Commission to a legislature-drawn map for 2026 through 2030 in response to Texas.
Question 1, which would have required photo ID, limited drop boxes to one per town and ended automatic absentee eligibility for older voters and voters with disabilities, was rejected.
Charter Question 6, which would have moved city elections to even-numbered years to raise turnout, was rejected.
Proposition 16 added an explicit constitutional ban on noncitizen voting, which state law already prohibited.
Third District Judge Dianna Gibson rejected the legislature's Map C, blocked SB 1011 and adopted the plaintiffs' Map 1 for the 2026 congressional elections under the restored Proposition 4 standards.

SB 12 banned ranked-choice voting in all Indiana elections. With Ohio's law of March 17, 2026, the National Conference of State Legislatures counts 19 states that prohibit it in some or all elections.

Nineteen states prohibit ranked-choice voting in some or all elections: Florida 2022, Tennessee 2022, Idaho 2023, Montana 2023, South Dakota 2023, Alabama 2024, Kentucky 2024, Louisiana 2024, Mississippi 2024, Missouri 2024, Oklahoma 2024, Arkansas 2025, Iowa 2025, Kansas 2025, North Dakota 2025, West Virginia 2025, Wyoming 2025, Indiana 2026 (SB 12, February 24) and Ohio 2026 (signed March 17). Missouri's prohibition is in its constitution (Amendment 7, 2024); the others are statutes, and their scope varies by state.
The Missouri Supreme Court held 4-3 that the constitution does not bar the legislature from redrawing congressional districts mid-decade.

In April 2026 Virginia joined the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, an agreement among states to award their electoral votes to the national popular-vote winner once members hold 270 electoral votes. Virginia brought the compact to 18 states plus D.C. and 222 electoral votes.
Voters approved a constitutional amendment letting the General Assembly redraw congressional districts through 2030 in response to other states' mid-decade maps.

Abbott v. League of United Latin American Citizens: the Supreme Court stayed the three-judge court's order blocking Texas's 2025 mid-decade map on December 4, 2025 (No. 25A608, 6 to 3), then summarily reversed that judgment on April 27, 2026 (No. 25-845, 6 to 3, without an opinion). The 2025 map governs the 2026 elections and, absent new litigation, the rest of the decade.

In Louisiana v. Callais the Supreme Court held 6 to 3 that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act did not require Louisiana's second majority-Black district, which made that map an unconstitutional racial gerrymander, and that Section 2 is violated only when the evidence supports a strong inference of intentional discrimination.

Florida House Bill 1-D of the 2026 Special Session D, enacted as Chapter 2026-229, redrew all 28 congressional districts in the middle of the decade, adopting plan EOGPCRP2026. Reporting at the time put the effect at three to four additional Republican seats. Equal Ground Education Fund sued in Leon County circuit court the day the bill was signed.

Tennessee's Second Extraordinary Session of 2026 passed three bills in one day: HB 7002 (Public Chapter 1) repealed the statutory ban on changing congressional districts between censuses, HB 7001 (Chapter 2) set the election mechanics, and HB 7003 with SB 7004 (Chapter 3) drew the map, splitting Memphis and Shelby County across three districts and ending the 9th's status as the state's only majority-Black district. The NAACP Tennessee State Conference sued within hours.
The Supreme Court of Virginia voided the April 21 redistricting referendum 4-3 because the legislature's first passage came after early voting had begun in the intervening 2025 election.
SB 121 enacted a new congressional map eliminating one of the state's two majority-Black districts.

Allen v. Milligan, No. 25A1314: after the three-judge district court found again on May 26, 2026 that Alabama's 2023 map was drawn to dilute Black votes, the Supreme Court stayed that order on June 2, 2026, an interim ruling. The 2023 map, without a second district where Black voters can elect a candidate of their choice, governs Alabama's 2026 elections in place of the court-ordered map used in 2024.
NRSC v. FEC struck down federal limits on spending that political parties coordinate with their candidates, overruling the Court's 2001 Colorado II decision.

Alaska Ballot Measure 1, on the August 18, 2026 primary ballot, reinstated state contribution limits of $2,000 per individual and $4,000 per group, per candidate per election, adjusted every ten years from 2031. It fills the gap left when a Ninth Circuit panel struck Alaska's 2006 limits in 2021 and the state declined to appeal, which left Alaska with no contribution limits for three election cycles. It does not reach independent-expenditure committees.

The Missouri Supreme Court held that the referendum power covers any act of the General Assembly, including a congressional map, so HB 1 is suspended and cannot be used in 2026 unless voters approve Proposition A.

The U.S. Supreme Court refused to let Missouri use its 2025 congressional map in November, leaving the state Supreme Court's referendum ruling and the 2022 map in place. A further order on September 25, 2026 (No. 26A388) directed that the 2022 map be used for the 2026 election and barred lower courts from requiring the 2025 map.

Ballot Measure 2 would repeal the top-four open primary and ranked-choice voting, restore party primaries and plurality general elections (the candidate with the most votes wins), and repeal the rule requiring disclosure of the true source of contributions of $2,000 or more.
Proposition A asks voters whether to approve HB 1 (2025) and its congressional map; a yes vote adopts the new map and a no vote keeps the 2022 districts.

Question 3 would replace party primaries for state, county and congressional offices with a single primary listing every candidate on one ballot, the top two advancing to the general election. It would take effect January 1, 2028, and would let parties endorse candidates and show the endorsement on the ballot.

repair.coding_note: Each row is coded by one of five labels. 'Toward voters' means the change widens who can register, vote or have a ballot counted, makes each vote weigh more equally, opens the contest that decides the seat, makes political money more limited or more visible, strengthens an independent check on officials, or adds to household security through automatic benefits. 'Away from voters' means the change does the reverse. 'Voters kept existing rules' means a ballot measure failed and the rules in force stayed, coded the same whichever way the measure would have moved power. 'Pending' means voters or courts have not yet decided. 'Mixed' means the change moved in both directions at once or left the rules in practice unchanged; the row's own note says which. Three rules apply across parties. A partisan redraw of district maps in the middle of a decade is coded away from voters whichever party draws it and whether or not voters approved it; a court order that blocks one is coded toward voters, and one that lets it take effect is coded away. A change that widens who takes part in the deciding round (open or all-party primaries) or lets voters rank candidates is coded toward voters, and a law or amendment that bans those options is coded away; readers may weigh these entries differently, and the reform profiles R-01 and R-02 rate confidence in their effect on moderation as low. A row's direction describes the rule's effect on who officials answer to and carries no judgment of the people or parties involved.

rows.what: The federal government lent money at low interest to farmer-owned cooperatives to string power lines down roads that private utilities had judged would never pay for themselves.
The GI Bill paid tuition and a living stipend for any returning veteran who enrolled in school, with no means test and no requirement to prove ability in advance.

rows.jurisdiction: Grand Rapids, Michigan, then most US municipalities
rows.what: A city commission voted to add a trace of fluoride to the municipal water supply, and the US Public Health Service measured the children's teeth before and after.
Congress created a dedicated gas-tax trust fund and built 41,000 miles of limited-access highway to a single national standard.
Congress enrolled every American over 65 in a single hospital insurance program and stood it up in under a year, before computers were common in government.
A new federal agency was given power to write binding minimum safety standards for every car sold in America, starting with seat belts and energy-absorbing steering columns.
A payroll tax funds a monthly check that arrives automatically at 62 or 65, indexed to inflation since 1972, with no application review of need.
Congress set national health-based air quality standards and required EPA to enforce them against states and industry regardless of cost.
EPA ordered refiners to take lead out of gasoline on a fixed schedule, over sustained industry objection, and finished the job in 1996.
The tax code pays a refundable credit that rises with earnings, so low-wage workers can receive money back even when they owe no income tax, delivered through the return they already file.
Congress capped total sulfur dioxide from power plants, handed out tradable allowances, and required continuous emissions monitors on every smokestack so the count could not be disputed.

The federal government buys childhood vaccines in bulk and gives them free to any provider treating an uninsured or Medicaid-eligible child, so a family's insurance status stops determining whether the child is vaccinated.

The Defense Department built a satellite navigation system. A Republican president opened it to civilian use, and a Democratic president switched off the deliberate degradation of the civilian signal, giving the whole economy a free and precise location service.

The Veterans Health Administration was rebuilt around primary care, a universal electronic health record and public performance measurement, at a time when almost no private hospital had any of the three.
The city raised its cigarette excise tax from 8 cents to 1.50 dollars a pack, banned smoking in every indoor workplace including bars, and ran a graphic television campaign.
After Hurricane Andrew destroyed 63,000 homes, Florida tightened its building codes and then replaced a patchwork of local codes with one statewide code with real inspection behind it.
The United States bought and delivered antiretroviral drugs at scale to countries where HIV treatment had been considered logistically impossible.
During the worst federal disaster failure in modern memory, one agency positioned its aircraft and crews outside the storm track in advance and started flying rescues before the water stopped rising.

A Republican governor and a Democratic legislature required everyone to carry health insurance, subsidized it for people who could not afford it, and got the uninsured rate to the lowest in the country.
California's workplace safety agency chose firms for inspection by lottery, which let researchers measure what an inspection does.
NOAA ran public supercomputers, satellites and hurricane hunter aircraft, and published its own forecast errors every year so anyone could check whether the forecasts were getting better.
For six months the Child Tax Credit was made fully refundable, raised, and paid out monthly, so families got the money whether or not they earned enough to owe tax.
Congress funds auditors who are independent of the agencies they audit, and they publish what they find whether or not the agency wants it published.
The Congressional Budget Office estimated how federal revenue changes when the IRS hires more enforcement staff, so the return on an enforcement dollar became a number Congress could score.
